structured_data_json_ld.description: Find out about things you can do yourself to stop or prevent hiccups.

hasPart.description: To stop hiccups, it may help to sip ice-cold water, bite on a lemon, taste vinegar or hold your breath for a short time.

hasPart.text: Although many people find these things helpful for stopping hiccups, there's no evidence that they work for everyone.

hasPart.headline: Do
hasPart.text:
• breathe into a paper bag (do not put it over your head)

  • pull your knees up to your chest and lean forward

  • sip ice-cold water

  • swallow some granulated sugar

  • bite on a lemon or taste vinegar

  • hold your breath for a short time

hasPart.headline: Don't
hasPart.text:
• do not drink alcoholic, fizzy or hot drinks

  • do not chew gum or smoke – these can cause you to swallow air

  • do not eat spicy food

  • do not eat food very quickly

  • do not eat or drink something very cold immediately after something hot

hasPart.headline: Things you can do yourself to stop or prevent hiccups

hasPart.description: It's not always obvious what causes hiccups. Sometimes they're triggered by stress, excitement, eating or drinking.

hasPart.text:
There's often no obvious reason why you get hiccups, but some people find certain things trigger their hiccups, such as:

  • stress
  • strong emotions, like excitement
  • eating and drinking

In rare cases, hiccups that last longer than 48 hours can be due to a medical condition or a medicine you're taking.

hasPart.headline: Why we get hiccups
See a GP if:
hasPart.text:
• hiccups last longer than 48 hours
  • hiccups come back very often and are affecting your life

hasPart.description: Most of the time hiccups go away without treatment. Sometimes changing a medicine you’re taking or treating the cause will stop the hiccups.

hasPart.text:
A GP will want to find out if your hiccups are caused by a health condition or medicine you're taking.

Treating the condition or changing your medicine should stop your hiccups.

If there's no obvious cause, they might be able to prescribe a medicine called chlorpromazine to treat your hiccups. This does not work for everyone.

hasPart.headline: Treatment for hiccups from a GP

hasPart.description: Hiccups are common and often go away on their own, there are things you can do yourself to help them go away. See a GP if they do not go away.
